div.p: Wath the prroliferation of scheduling algorithms there is a growing need to test these schedulers for their validity not jusi! at design time but also as the system evolves. This implaes that the schedulability analysis has to be robust. In thas study, we identify a few often posed questions that address the robustness of schedulability analyses. First these questions are dealt in the context of uniprocessor systems and then we handle some of their eitensions an a more general context of end-to-end systlems. We show that these questions are closely related to a more general problem. We present a solution to this problem. A n intuative proof of correctness and optimality of the solution technique are presented.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: With the amount of research that has been spent in the area of scheduling [la] in real-time systems, it seems but obvious that a practitioner today would be overwhelmed b:y the number of possible choices. Of these scheduler:$, static fixed priority schedulers have played a predominant role because of their relative stability 131 and low run-time overhead. While such properties have aided their prominence, their widespread use has also raised concerns.

Of this melange of static fixed priority schedulers the rate monotonic scheduling mechanism (RMS) is the most widely researched [5]. The deterministic nature of this scheduling mechanism comes, in terms of guaranteeing that a given task set will be schedulable provided some utilization bounds are honored. However, the utilization bound is too restrictive to be of much practical significance. A stronger argument in favor of this scheduling mechanism is that while this bound absolutely guarantees the schedulability of a task-set, failure to meet this bound does not necessarily mean that the task set would be infeasible (or non-schedulable) .

Researchers have therefore suggested using a more detailed analysis in cases where this base schedulability test fails [l, 7, lo]. We refer to this detailed analysis as schedulabbility analysis (note that this analysis is not specific to RMS but is applicable to any static fixed priority scheduling mechanism in general) and in 'This work is sponsored by a grant from NASA (NAG-I-
this paper we propose some extensions to the analysis that help us in addressing some nascent issues in design and maintenance of complex real time systems.

Though the discussion in this paper is based on the problem of schedulability in uniprocessor systems, we observe that current complex real time systems are far from being simple systems where the only schedulable entity is the processor. With a growth in complexity of real time systems it has become important to view them as systems with a set of schedulable entities (we refer to as components) that are used by tasks as a part of their execution. This view brings in its wake a need for decomposition of tasks into subtasks with each subtask being assigned to a component. A designer now has a responsibility not just to meet individual subtask requirements but to satisfy the endto-end requirements of the task in question. The endto-end requirement of primary concern to us here is the deadline (The release time is the other end-to-end requirement). Systems where such is the scenario will henceforth be referred to as end-to-end systems.

The paper is organized as follows. In the next section we define a general scaling problem which will help answer some questions involved in real time system design and maintenance. Section 3 gives details of the solution to this problem supported by an intuitive proof followed by and example. In section 4 we discuss this problem in the context of end-to-end systems and section 5 summarizes the results by showing how the general scaling problem helps answer the questions posed in section 2. Conclusions and future work are given in section 6.

div.head: Problem Statement
div.p: Following are some of the questions that are often asked during the design and maintenance of real time systems:

Often schedulability analysis in real-time systems is done off-line and the individual task execution times are assumed to be constant. However, we are often faced with the situation where, as the system is evolving, the execution times of the tasks may change. Such changes could result in increased computation and communication requirements of tasks. It is tedious and impractical to perform the schedulability analysis every time there is a change. The question is:
(i) By how much can a task execution time be increased maintaining its schedulability?
e Task execution time estimation

Using the worst-case execution times of tasks for schedulability analysis is a rather pessimistic approach. In most applications, the worst case path (through the code) is not the most frequently traversed path. In order to handle this problem, we can make use of the statistical estimation techniques for finding the execution time. There should be some way of accommodating the information about the variance in the schedulability analysis. The question is:
(ii) What is the maximum variance in task execution time that can be tolerated?

0 Application Portability Execution time of a task is a function of the speed of the processor on which the application is to be run. Therefore, depending upon the speed of the target processor, the execution time could vary. Schedulability analysis is performed making some assumptions about the target processor speed. The question of concern is:

(iii) Is the schedulability analysis valid even when the target processor changes? 0 Fault Tolerance A commonly used approach to fault-tolerance involves providing for a degraded mode of operation during a failure. Such a mode of operation is often achieved by a fall back component that is not as efficient (performance-wise) as the original component and therefore could imply that the response time of tasks using the component under question could be increased. The question is:
(iv) What characteristics of fall-back components make them suitable for maintaining the system fault-tolerant?

0 System Improvement With ever changing costs of system components, sometimes the most favored choice is not the fastest choice but one that justifies its cost. System improvement could involve replacing costly components by ones that meet the standards and are cheap a t the same time meeting the system performance requirements. Further, such component changes reflect as execution time changes to only a sub-set of the various subtasks We will talk about task decomposition later). T b e question is:

The above stated problems are related to a more fundamental problem which is an extension to schedulability analysis: Given a schedulable task set consisting of n tasks T : (T1,TZ ,..., Tn}l, and a subset of the tasks S. Find an optimal common scaling factor (sf) by which the execution times of the tasks in the subset S can be scaled, without affecting (or invalidating) the schedulability of the task-set T .

A clarification is due regarding the relationship between the above problem and the issue of scalability. The above statement of the problem talks about finding a common scaling factor giving an impression that all tasks will be scaled by the same amount (whenever scaling occurs), this is however not true. For a given task this factor only gives an upper bound for its scaling. For example, if the common scaling factor obtained is sf then a given task's execution time can be scaled by a factor f where 1 5 f _< sf.
We lay down the assumptions made in the formulation of the general problem stated above.

We characterize a task by the following parameters: execution time ci; periodicity pi and deadline di. 0 A schedulable task set means a task set which when scheduled by the assumed preemptive (either a static fixed priority scheduling algorithm or a dynamic scheduling algorithm) scheduling algorithm will have all of its task deadlines met for all possible task phasings. 0 A fixed priority scheduling algorithm can be simply viewed as a priority ordering of the tasks in the task set. Taking this perspective the order in which the tasks execute can be taken t o be the order of their priorities. Note that we have introduced the parameter of priority to keep the scheduler as general as possible. For example if the scheduler is a rate-monotonic scheduling algorithm then the priorities of the tasks will be in the reverse order of the periodicities. We can also derive the task priorities as a weighted function of the various task parameters [13]. Therefore, from here onwards we will assume that the tasks are or- dered in the non-increasing order (a simple transformation can convert this non-increasing order to a strictly decreasing order) of their priorities, i.e., the first task TI is the highest priority task and priority of task Tj is greater than Ti if j < i.

as being optimal, we mean that any larger sca \ ing factor would result in a t least one of the tasks in the task set missing its deadline. idle (i.e., there is no idle time left in the schedule). Therefore even after scaling the task-set, it is possible to increase the computation time of one or more of the tasks but not all of the tasks in the sub-set.
a When we refer to a change in a task execution time, we assume a scale-up and not an addition. However, we note that the problem of proportional addition can be phrased on the same lines as scaling.

We concern ourselves mainly with a static fixed priority scheduling mechanism like the rate monotonic scheduling algorithm. This is because the above problem has a rather trivial solution when we assume a dynamic preemptive scheduling algorithm like the earliest-deadlinle first. div.head: Task System Model
div.p: In the treatment of the previous section we have conveniently assumed that there are n tasks which demand only one component, viz., the processor. While the assumption has allowed us to demonstrate a solution for the proposed problem, it is too restrictive to be of any practical significance. In this section we take a more practical approach to modeling tasks in endto-end real-time systems (both uniprocessor systems and distributed systems).

We perceive a task x as a sequence of sub-tasks, Til -+ --+ ... 4 Tip, where each sub-task, Tij executes on a component. Further, each sub-task uses the partial results of prior sub-tasks in its sequence. A task T, has the following parameters: ci: The total execution time of the task (this includes all the subtasks that comprise the task. The execution time for the k'th sub-task of task Tj is given by c ; k ) ; p ; : The task as a whole has a period meaning that only the first sub-task Ti1 is sure to repeat every pi units of time; di: A deadline for the whole task.

There can be many bases for task decomposition, however, the one of concern to us here is the one that involves component use. A component is a generic term which refers to any schedulable entity (processor, communication interface, resource etc.). We assume that if a section of code involves the use of a particular component, that section3 is identified as a sub-task with its own processing requirements (on the component in question). We observed that this basis for task decomposition can be accommodated along with any other criteria. For example, we can view the process of task decomposition as a step-wise mechanism (with each step further sub-dividing sub-tasks or coalescing sub-tasks) in which the last step involves decomposition on the basis of component use. We note that tasks in distributed systems could span over multiple processors (nodes) and therefore each such processor can be identified as a component that the task uses. Assuming that we have a deterministic allocation mechanism (based on a static fixed priority allocation) for the underlying network, we can treat the network also as a component. We understand that this is a restrictive assumption because most current multiaccess network protocols are not based on static fixed priority allocation. However, the assumption does have its support from work reported in [4, 61.
Other components could be devices, sensors, actuators etc.

The system itself is modeled as comprising of a set of r components, { R I , R2,. . .,E,-}. The particular component that the execution of a sub-task x j depends on is obtained by the function, Res(Tij).

div.head: General Scaling Problem
div.p: The general scaling problem now changes in the following way. We can now pose the question from the following two perspectives: (i) a change in the components in use, implying that all sub-tasks that use these component undergo scaling. or (ii) for each component that undergoes a change, only a sub-set of the sub-tasks that use it are affected by the change.
The first of these perspectives can be posed as the following problem:

Given the following: a schedulable decomposed task-set T, a component-set R, a mapping from T to R and a priority assignment (possibly at the sub-task level); What changes to a particular component Rj can the task-set tolerate with regards to the schedulability of the task-set.

We have laid dlown the foundation for building a solution to this problem in the previous sub-sections. A component change can now be viewed as an isolated event and can be handled on the same lines as described in the previous section. For example, in order to study the possible changes that can be tolerated in the component say Rk , we have to find a common sealing factor for all sub-tasks (represented as Tk) that run on this component. The second perspective can be posed as the following problem:

Given the following: a schedulable decomposed task-set T, a component-set R, a mapping from T to R and a priority assignment (possibly at the sub-task level); By how much can a sub-set of all sub-tasks5 that use a component Rk be scaled so that the schedulability of the task-set is maintained.

The solution to this problem is on the same lines as the previous one except that we now have the subset Sk which is not, the same as Tk. Note that in both the problem statements above we talk about a particular component Rk, however, the extension to handle a set of components (say I ? We observe that the choice of the heuristic in deriving sub-task deadlines from task deadlines plays a very crucial role in the effectiveness of the schedulability analysis in end-to-end systems. We are currently investigating different heuristics that would allow us to solve the schedulability analysis problem keeping in mind our ultimate goal of achieving optimal scaling factors.

div.head: Results
div.p: We now discuss how a solution to the general scaling problem ai~swers the questions posed in section 2. Relevance to scalability is straightforward. As a system evolves., more and more functionality is added resulting in eitlher increasing the number of tasks (for e.g., Addition of a new radar system could cause an increase in radar related tasks) or adding enhancements to the already existing tasks (for e.g., increment in the number of flights monitored by an air traffic control system), or both. The first choice would imply that the schedulability analysis has to be performed again, however the second choice would reflect itself as a scaling of the execiation time of the task in question.

The difficulty in finding the execution times of prorams in general and real-time programs in particular b l h as been emphasized by many researchers in the past. It has belcome imperative that any such estimations have to b'e qualified by taking into consideration the variance. relates to the problem of testing. Due to the life critical conditions under which real-time systems operate, it is often difficult or in most cases impossible to test the final system in operation. A reasonable alternative to testing the system is to build a prototype of the system. In order to facilitate a thorough (possibly exhaustive) testing we could build the prototype to be a scaled up (faster) realization of the target system. We can now do a schedulability analysis of the prototype system and seek to extend the results to the target system. Clearly, the schedulability analysis holds if the target system is faster than the prototype. If however the target system is slower (which is often the case), then we observe that such a change in processor speed (and other architectural parameters) would reflect as an increase in execution time. Thus, the problem reduces to the general scalability problem.

div.head: Conclusions and Future W o r k
div.p: We have identified some important issues that a real time system designer often faces during both the design and maintenance of systems. We have shown that these issues are closely related to a more general problem called the scaling problem. We have successfully demonstrated a technique (proved to be effective) to solve this general problem that involves finding a common scaling factor that preserves the schedulability of a task-set in end-to-end systems. An example to demonstrate the technique with its various possibilities is presented.

The critical instant assumption is true in general but is a pessimistic view to schedulability analysis that ignores the information about the arrival times that are of a great practical importance [l, 111. Therefore in the next stage of our work we are trying to incorporate arrival information into our analysis. We

have not yet thoroughly investigated the applicability of our solution to the general scaling problem in the context of end-to-end systems. We are also working on a more detailed classification of end-to-end systems on the lines followed by Bettati [2] in order to derive more specific results (application wise) for the problems posed in this paper.
